title: Product Descriptions for People and AI
h1: Product descriptions for people and AI
desc: Write product descriptions that answer what a buyer asks: what it is, who it is for, the facts that decide, and how it differs. Clear facts help people and tools.
lead: A good product description states what the product is, who it suits and the facts that matter, before it sells. The same facts help a customer decide and help a tool describe the product correctly.
body:
Most product descriptions are written to sound attractive. The ones that get quoted are written to be useful. When a shopper asks "which blender is good for small families", the useful description is the one that lets a person, or a tool, answer with confidence.

Lead with what it is

The first sentence should name the product and say what it is for. Compare:

Before. "Experience the joy of effortless blending."

After. "The Example 600 is a 600-watt countertop blender with a 1.5-litre jug, made for smoothies, sauces and crushed ice for two to four people."

The second sentence contains facts. They are my invented example values, so use your own real specifications.

Include the facts buyers compare

Think about what a buyer checks before choosing, and put those facts in plain text near the top:

  • Size, weight, capacity, materials.
  • Compatibility: what it works with.
  • What is in the box.
  • Warranty and return terms.
  • Price, currency and availability, kept up to date.

Use a simple specifications table

FieldExample value
Product name (full)Example 600 Blender
Suitable for2 to 4 people
Power600 W
WarrantyFill in your real terms

A table makes comparison easy for a reader and keeps each fact next to its label.

Write the full name

Write "the Example 600 blender" rather than "it" or "our product". When a sentence is quoted on its own, the pronoun has no meaning. This is the same rule I apply in all content: a passage should make sense when lifted out of its page.

Be honest about limits

Say who the product is not for: "not suitable for hot liquids above 70 degrees", if that is true. Honest limits reduce returns and build trust. Never write a claim you cannot support, such as "the best" or "number one", unless you can show the basis.

Structured data

Product structured data is a documented way to describe a product to machines. If you use it, the values must match what the page shows: same name, same price, same availability. Google states that no special markup is required for its AI features, so treat it as an accurate description. Read about it in the schema entry.

A quick checklist before you publish

  1. Read the first sentence alone. Does it say what the product is and who it is for?
  2. Check every number. Compare each size, price and warranty term with your real data.
  3. Remove empty adjectives. "Premium", "amazing" and "high quality" say nothing unless you add proof.
  4. Look at it on a phone. Most shoppers will, and the specifications must stay readable.
  5. Set a review date. Put a reminder to check the page every quarter, because outdated prices and stock status are the most common errors I find.

Reviews and questions

Add real customer questions and answers near the product. They often contain the exact words buyers use. For more on writing answers that can be quoted, read answer-first content.

To see whether shoppers' questions mention your store at all, try the free visibility test.
faq: How long should a product description be?
Long enough to state the facts a buyer needs. A short paragraph plus a specifications table is often enough.
Should I copy the supplier's description?
Avoid it. Identical text appears on many sites. Write your own using the facts you verified.
Google says no special markup is required for its AI features. If you add it, keep every value identical to the visible page.
